extracted.subtask_description: Conventions and practical standards for composing newspaper stories and dispatches (datelines, bylines, leads, attribution, use of figures, scene-setting, balance, official titles, etc.) as exemplified by wartime reporting and feature pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and source attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dateline giving the location and date, followed by the news service tag when appropriate (example: "LUNENBURG, Nova Scotia, May 23—(AP)").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the city, region, and date at the start of the story for immediate context; append the wire-service or source marker such as (AP) or (Delayed) when the dispatch is from a news agency or delayed. This orients the reader and signals provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byline / reporter credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Give reporter credit at the top of the story (example: "By JOHN FERRIS -").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the author's name prominently to indicate responsibility and authority for the report, especially for feature and on-the-scene pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid scene-setting lead / human-interest hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with a vivid, character-focused scene to engage readers (example lead: "George Rhuland, tall, heavy and old, climbed stiffly down the steep stairs... cupping his big hands, roared an order...").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with concrete sensory detail or an action that humanizes the story subject; use this as the narrative anchor for a feature or local-interest story rather than a dry summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precise numerical details and statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify scale and impact with specific numbers (examples: "Flora Albert had lost 21 of her 28 men", population and catch figures like "population is 2,830", "45,000,000 pounds").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide exact figures where available to lend credibility and convey magnitude. Use measurements, counts, years, and weights to make abstract effects concrete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct quotes with clear attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Include direct quotations and identify the speaker (examples: police notification text, statements by officials and private citizens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quoted material to show voice and provide primary-source evidence. Always attribute quotes (name and, when relevant, title or role). When quoting official instructions or notifications, reproduce wording accurately to show tenor and force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background and historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide historical or background information that situates the current event (examples: reference to the famous Bluenose, shipbuilding since 1900, prior incidents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add concise backstory or historical details that help readers understand significance: past achievements, prior losses, long-term trends, or institutional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological sequencing of events
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrate incidents in logical order from sighting/trigger through actions taken and outcomes (example: U-boat sighted, plane dove, depth charges released, U-boat damaged, then destroyed by gunfire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For action stories and reports of incidents, lay out the timeline clearly so cause and effect are understandable; include immediate consequences and later confirmations when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of official titles and formal identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify people by name and office/rank (examples: "Secretary of the Treasury", "Lieutenant Gordon R. Fiss", "Prime Minister Churchill").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full titles or ranks for officials and military personnel on first reference to establish authority and context. This aids reader comprehension and precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenting multiple perspectives and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Include differing viewpoints and reactions within coverage (examples: Trotsky's widow's denunciation vs. supportive statements by Diego Rivera; AF of L and C.I.O. positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When controversies or policy decisions are involved, present principal opposing or complementary perspectives to give readers a rounded understanding; attribute opinions clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, informative headlines and subheads
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concise headlines and subheads to summarize key points (examples: "Builder", "Let Each Furnish Full Share of Metals, Says Sen. Revercomb.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft headlines that capture the gist or the most newsworthy angle. Use subheads to break long copy into readable sections and highlight secondary facts or quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetical clarifications and source notations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parentheticals for brief clarifications and to note source or status of copy (examples: "(AP)", "(Delayed)").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert short parenthetical tags for wire service, delay status, or other immediate clarifications without interrupting flow; reserve longer explanations for the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report operational details for drills/exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering drills or preparedness exercises, list objectives, scope, participants, and outcomes (example mock air-raid: "first objective was the Loop", "200,000 civilian defense workers", "185 planes" and assessment of success).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the plan, scale (numbers of people and equipment), targets, procedures used, and official assessments of effectiveness so readers can judge preparedness and results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize human impact and community effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight consequences for local people and institutions (examples: "sea deaths have left 45 children fatherless", mention of churches, banks, hotels lost or affected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include human-interest details—casualties, orphaned children, lost businesses—to show how events translate into personal and communal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report on censorship and official evasion with specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe censorship actions and note authorities' reluctance to provide legal citations (examples: censor stopped dispatches quoting opposition speeches; police notification warning against "distribution of alarmist news" without chapter-and-verse citation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting suppression or restrictions, include the language used by authorities and point out when legal or procedural bases are omitted or vague; this helps readers assess legitimacy and scope of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of local color, dialect, and authentic voice when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey local flavor and speech patterns to add authenticity (example: noting a "curious accent" that is neither Nova Scotian nor German).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In feature and on-the-scene reporting, judiciously use local expressions, accents, or idioms to enrich narrative, while not caricaturing subjects; attribute such remarks and explain context for wider readers.
